summary: The evidence-based psychology of sustaining performance over the long haul —

facts.text: The evidence-based psychology of sustaining performance over the long haul - your own and your team's - without burning out. Ten constructs, organized into three layers:
What drives effort - mindset, grit, achievement goals, regulatory focus.
What sustains it in the moment - flow, self-efficacy, self-regulation.
What protects against collapse - stress appraisal & coping, burnout, recovery & resilience.

The throughline: high performance is not a trait you have or lack; it is a state you engineer - through how you frame ability, structure goals, manage attention and arousal, appraise stress, and recover. Each section gives a self-management note (sustaining your own performance) and a team / coaching note (leading and developing others).

This field has a serious replication problem, and this skill is honest about it: two of its most famous constructs (growth-mindset interventions, ego depletion) have weak or failed-to-replicate evidence, and a third (grit) is largely redundant with an older trait. Use the strong constructs confidently; treat the contested ones as heuristics, not laws. Where the science is thin, the section says so.

facets.title: 1. Implicit theories of ability — growth vs fixed mindset (Dweck)

facts.text: Core idea. People hold an implicit "lay theory" about whether ability is fixed (an entity theory - you have a fixed amount of intelligence/talent) or malleable (an incremental theory - ability grows with effort and strategy). A fixed mindset makes effort feel like evidence of low ability and makes failure identity-threatening, so people avoid challenge and disengage. A growth mindset reframes effort and failure as the mechanism of getting better, so people seek challenge and persist (Dweck - Mindset Works).
Be honest about the effect size. This is the single most over-sold construct in popular performance psychology. The Sisk et al. (2018) two meta-analyses are the key correction:
Across 273 studies / ~365,000 people, mindset accounted for only ~1% of the variance in academic achievement (a weak correlation).
Across 43 intervention studies / ~57,000 people, growth-mindset interventions produced a standardized mean difference of d ≈ 0.08 - very small (Sisk et al. 2018, Psychological Science; PubMed).
Moderator finding: low-SES and academically at-risk people benefited more, which is the strongest remaining case for targeted intervention.

The debate is live: Yeager & Dweck (2020) argue that for a cheap, scalable intervention even a small average effect concentrated in the right subgroup is meaningful; Macnamara & Burgoyne (2022) re-analyzed and still found weak, inconsistent effects (Macnamara & Burgoyne 2022, PDF%20-%20Do%20Growth%20Mindset%20Interventions%20Impact%20Students%E2%80%99%20Academic%20Achievement.pdf)).

Takeaway: mindset is a real and useful frame, but it is not a high-impact intervention you can sprinkle on a team and expect performance to jump. Treat "praise effort/strategy, not innate talent" as a sound default, not a silver bullet.

Self-management note. Catch fixed-mindset self-talk ("I'm just not a numbers person") and convert it to a strategy question ("what approach haven't I tried yet?"). The value is in keeping yourself in hard problems rather than fleeing them - not in expecting a mindset shift to manufacture skill you haven't built.

Team / coaching note. Praise process (strategy, effort, choices), not the person ("you're so smart"). Person-praise installs a fixed mindset and makes the next failure threatening. Critically, do not weaponize "growth mindset" as a way to blame people for outcomes ("you just need a better mindset") - that is a "false growth mindset" and it is demotivating. Pair the frame with actual resources, feedback, and time to improve.

facets.title: 2. Grit (Duckworth) — and why it's mostly conscientiousness

facts.text: Core idea. Grit is perseverance and passion for long-term goals - the tendency to sustain effort and interest over years despite failure and plateaus, measured by the Grit Scale across two facets: perseverance of effort and consistency of interest (Duckworth et al. 2007, summary).

Be honest about the critique. The Credé, Tynan & Harms (2017) meta-analysis (584 effect sizes, 88 samples, ~66,800 people) is the essential corrective and is often called the "jangle fallacy" paper (two different names for the same thing):
Grit correlates with conscientiousness at ρ ≈ .84 - so strong that grit is arguably redundant with a personality trait psychology has measured for decades.
Grit explains almost no incremental variance in performance once you control for conscientiousness.
The higher-order "grit" structure (combining the two facets) was not confirmed; the two facets behave differently.

Perseverance of effort carries essentially all the predictive value; consistency of interest predicts little. So "keep working hard" matters; "never change your passion" does not (Credé et al. 2017, JPSP, PDF; PubMed).
Implication: grit interventions likely have only weak effects on performance.

Takeaway: the useful, evidence-backed half of grit is perseverance of effort, which is just the actionable edge of conscientiousness. The "stick with the same passion for a decade" half is not well supported and can be actively bad advice (it discourages adaptive pivoting).

Self-management note. Optimize for sustained effort on the current important goal, not for never changing direction. Re-evaluating and pivoting is not a grit failure - consistency-of-interest is the facet that doesn't predict success.

Team / coaching note. Don't screen or label people by "grit." It mostly re-measures conscientiousness, and using it as a virtue can shade into blaming people for structural problems (bad systems, unrealistic load). Reward visible perseverance through difficulty; never use "lacks grit" as a performance verdict.

Core idea. Flow is the state of complete absorption in an activity, where action and awareness merge, self-consciousness drops, time distorts, and the activity becomes autotelic (rewarding in itself) (Positive Psychology - Csikszentmihalyi).

The challenge-skill balance (the flow channel). Flow occurs when the challenge of the task and your skill level are both high and roughly balanced. Plot challenge (y) against skill (x): the diagonal band where they match is the flow channel. Off-diagonal you get the failure modes:
High challenge + low skill → anxiety.
Low challenge + high skill → boredom.
Low + low → apathy. As skill grows, the task must get harder to stay in the channel - flow is a moving target (Yu-kai Chou - Flow Theory & the 9 components).

Antecedents (the conditions you can engineer). The reliable preconditions are (1) clear, proximal goals and (2) immediate, unambiguous feedback, on top of the challenge-skill match. Characteristics during flow include intense concentration, a sense of control, merging of action and awareness, and loss of self-consciousness (Investigating the Flow Experience, PMC). An autotelic personality disposes some people to enter flow more readily.

Self-management note. Manufacture the antecedents: protect an uninterrupted block, define a single concrete sub-goal for the session, and create a fast feedback loop (tests, a checklist, a draft you can see growing). Tune difficulty - if anxious, shrink the task; if bored, raise the bar. Notifications are the single biggest flow-killer because they reset concentration and break the feedback loop.

Team / coaching note. Design work to keep people in the channel: match assignment difficulty to growing skill (stretch, don't drown or bore), make goals concrete, and shorten feedback latency (frequent, specific feedback beats an annual review). Meeting-fragmented calendars make team flow nearly impossible - defend maker-time blocks as a performance lever, not a perk.

facets.title: 4. Self-efficacy (Bandura) — the belief that you can

facts.text: Core idea. Self-efficacy is the task-specific belief that you can execute the actions required to produce a given outcome ("I can do this"). It predicts which goals people set, how much effort they invest, and how they persist under setback - often more strongly than actual ability does (Simply Psychology - self-efficacy).
Distinguish it from two neighbors (this matters):

Self-esteem = global self-worth ("I am a good/worthy person"). Self-efficacy is domain-specific competence belief, not worth. You can have high efficacy at coding and low at public speaking; self-esteem doesn't move that way.

Outcome expectancy = belief that an action leads to an outcome. Efficacy is belief that you can perform the action. You can believe studying produces good grades (outcome expectancy) yet doubt you can make yourself study (low efficacy).
The four sources (in order of power):

Mastery experiences - actually succeeding at the task. By far the strongest source; nothing builds efficacy like a track record of overcoming difficulty. Easy wins build fragile efficacy; wins through effort build durable efficacy.
Vicarious experience - watching a similar other succeed ("if someone like me can, I can"). Model similarity is what makes it work.
Verbal/social persuasion - credible encouragement. Weaker, and bounded by the persuader's credibility; empty cheerleading backfires.

Physiological & affective states - how you interpret your own arousal. A pounding heart read as "I'm choking" lowers efficacy; read as "I'm fired up" raises it. Weakest source but a useful lever via reappraisal (Bandura's 4 sources - Yu-kai Chou; PsychologyNotesHQ).

> Cross-reference: behavior-change-psychology touches self-efficacy as one input > into a customer's decisional balance for adoption. This skill owns the construct > itself - the four sources and how to build efficacy in yourself and your team.

Self-management note. Build efficacy bottom-up: sequence tasks so you bank genuine mastery experiences on an upward difficulty curve, rather than starting with the scariest thing and failing. Before a high-stakes moment, reframe arousal ("this is energy/readiness," not "this is panic").

Team / coaching note. Use all four sources deliberately: (1) engineer early wins through real challenge (mastery is strongest); (2) show peer models - a similar teammate who did it beats an expert who makes it look effortless; (3) make encouragement specific and credible, tied to evidence; (4) normalize nerves before stretch assignments so people don't read arousal as proof they can't. Stretch assignments are the single most effective development tool because a mastery experience under genuine difficulty is what builds durable confidence.

facets.title: 5. Achievement goal theory — mastery vs performance, 2x2 and 3x2

facts.text: Core idea. Why you pursue achievement shapes outcomes. The classic split:
Mastery goals - aim to develop competence / learn the task (self-referenced standard).
Performance goals - aim to demonstrate competence relative to others (normative standard) (Grading for Growth - achievement goal orientations).
The 2x2 framework (Elliot & McGregor, 2001). Crossing the mastery/performance definition with an approach vs avoidance valence gives four goals:
Mastery-approach - strive to learn and improve. Most consistently linked to positive outcomes (deep learning, intrinsic interest, persistence).
Performance-approach - strive to outperform others. Mixed: can boost grades and effort but is fragile and tied to extrinsic, contingent motivation.
Mastery-avoidance - strive not to fail to learn / not to lose skill (e.g., a declining expert). Generally maladaptive.
Performance-avoidance - strive not to look incompetent. The most maladaptive - drives anxiety, self-handicapping, and withdrawal (Elliot & McGregor 2001 - Semantic Scholar).

The 3x2 framework (Elliot, Murayama & Pekrun, 2011). Splits "mastery" into task-based (did I do the task well?) and self-based (did I do better than my past self?), each crossed with approach/avoidance, yielding six goals (task-approach, task-avoidance, self-approach, self-avoidance, other-approach, other-avoidance) (3x2 model - Frontiers; 3x2 systematic review/meta-analysis, PMC).

Self-management note. Frame your own hard goals as mastery-approach ("get better at X," "beat my last attempt") rather than performance-avoidance ("don't look bad in the review"). The avoidance frame predicts anxiety and self-handicapping; the mastery frame predicts persistence and learning from failure.

Team / coaching note. The climate you set pushes people toward a goal type. A purely normative, ranked, comparative environment (stack-ranking, leaderboards, "top performer of the month") nudges people into performance goals - and, for those who doubt they'll win, into performance-avoidance (the most toxic quadrant: fear, self-handicapping, hiding mistakes). Build a mastery climate: reward improvement and learning, frame goals against the person's own prior level, and make it safe to attempt hard things and fail. Use comparison sparingly and only where it genuinely motivates the specific person.

facets.title: 6. Regulatory focus theory (Higgins) — promotion vs prevention

facts.text: Core idea. People pursue goals through one of two motivational systems (Regulatory focus theory - Wikipedia; Higgins 1998, PDF):

Promotion focus - oriented to gains, ideals, growth, aspirations. Driven by eagerness; sensitive to the presence/absence of positive outcomes; pursues "ideal self" goals (hopes, what you want to be). Favors speed, risk, and exploration.

Prevention focus - oriented to security, duties, oughts, avoiding losses. Driven by vigilance; sensitive to the presence/absence of negative outcomes; pursues "ought self" goals (responsibilities, what you should do). Favors accuracy, caution, and thoroughness.
Focus is both a chronic disposition and a situationally inducible state - you can frame a task to evoke either.

Regulatory fit. Motivation intensifies and the activity "feels right" when the means of pursuit match the focus: promotion-focused people are energized by eager, gain-framed strategies; prevention-focused people by vigilant, loss-framed ones. Fit increases engagement, persistence, and even perceived value - in one study, fit raised willingness-to-pay for the same mug by ~40–70% (Yu-kai Chou - regulatory focus; BehavioralEconomics.com).

Self-management note. Match the frame to the work. For creative/exploratory or growth work, adopt a promotion frame ("what could we gain / what's the upside"). For quality-critical, security, or compliance work - where errors are costly - adopt a prevention frame ("what must not go wrong"). Mis-fit (a prevention person forced to "move fast and break things," or a promotion person buried in checklists) drains motivation.

Team / coaching note. Frame goals and feedback to fit the person and the task. A promotion-focused report responds to opportunity and aspiration ("here's how this moves you up"); a prevention-focused report responds to responsibility and risk ("here's what we'd lose if this slips"). Same message, different framing, very different motivational pull. Also staff to fit: put prevention-focused people on accuracy-critical work and promotion-focused people on exploration - and frame the mission accordingly.

facets.title: 7. Self-regulation, willpower & self-control — and the ego-depletion problem

facts.text: Core idea. Self-regulation is steering your own behavior toward goals against competing impulses and distractions - the engine behind every other construct here.

The ego-depletion claim - and why to be skeptical. The dominant model for two decades (Baumeister) held that willpower is a limited resource that depletes with use, like a muscle that fatigues, so exerting self-control on Task A leaves you worse at Task B. This is the famous "ego depletion" effect - and it is one of the headline casualties of the replication crisis:
Carter et al. (2015) re-analyzed the literature correcting for publication bias and concluded the likely true effect was near zero.

Hagger et al. (2016) ran a preregistered multilab replication across 23 labs (N ≈ 2,141) and failed to find the effect - no medium or even small ego-depletion effect (Hagger et al. 2016, Perspectives on Psychological Science; PDF).

Caveat in both directions: some argue the specific depleting task used was weak, and the construct isn't disproven so much as not robustly demonstrated. But the strong "willpower is a finite fuel tank" story should not be treated as established fact.

> Cross-reference: behavioral-decision-making covers ego depletion as a decision- > effect and carries the broader replication-crisis methodology (preregistration, > publication bias, p-hacking). Go there for the meta-science; this section covers > the performance implication.
What replaces it. Two more durable ideas:

Motivation/attention model (Inzlicht): apparent "depletion" is better explained as shifts in motivation and attention over time, not a drained resource - you disengage from effortful control when something feels less worth it.

Implicit theories of willpower (Job, Dweck, Walton): people who believe willpower is limited show depletion-like patterns; those who believe it's not limited often don't. The belief partly creates the effect.

Self-management note. Stop budgeting a mythical "willpower tank." Instead, reduce the need for self-control through environment design (remove the distraction, pre-commit, use implementation intentions - see behavior-change-psychology), and protect motivation/attention (rest, meaning, single-tasking). Fatigue is real; a depleting "willpower fuel gauge" is not well supported.

Team / coaching note. Don't design work on the assumption that people have a fixed daily ration of self-control to spend. Performance dips usually signal eroded motivation, unclear priorities, or genuine fatigue/overload, not a depleted willpower battery. Fix the environment and the meaning, not the person's "discipline."

facets.title: 8. Stress & coping (Lazarus & Folkman) — appraisal is everything

facts.text: Core idea - the transactional model. Stress is not in the event; it's in the transaction between person and situation, mediated by appraisal. The same deadline is energizing to one person and crushing to another because they appraise it differently (Transactional model - EBSCO; Mindtools).

Primary appraisal - "Is this at stake for me, and is it harm/loss, threat, or challenge?" Crucially, a stressor can be appraised as a threat (potential for loss/harm, → fear, defensiveness, narrowed thinking) or as a challenge (potential for growth/gain that's demanding but masterable, → energized, approach-oriented). Same demand, opposite physiology and performance.
Secondary appraisal - "Can I cope? What are my resources and options?" Your appraised coping capacity is what flips threat into challenge.
Two coping families:
Problem-focused coping - act on the stressor itself (plan, gather info, remove the obstacle, renegotiate the deadline). Most adaptive when the situation is controllable.

Emotion-focused coping - regulate the distress (reframe, seek support, acceptance, distraction). Most adaptive when the situation is uncontrollable and you must endure it. Maladaptive emotion-focused coping (denial, rumination, avoidance, substances) is where this family goes wrong.
The art is matching coping to controllability - problem-focus what you can change, emotion-focus what you can't, and accurately telling the two apart.

> Cross-reference: the mechanics of emotion-focused coping - reappraisal vs > suppression, Gross's process model of emotion regulation - live in > emotion-and-affect-psychology. This section owns the appraisal-and-coping frame; > that skill owns the regulation toolkit.

Self-management note. Run the two appraisals explicitly under pressure: (1) reappraise threat as challenge where honest - focus on what's masterable and what you stand to gain, not only what you could lose (this is the single most useful move; it changes your physiology toward approach); (2) match coping to control - make a concrete plan for the controllable parts, and use acceptance/ support/reframing for the parts you can't change. Pure emotion-focus on a controllable problem (venting instead of acting) prolongs the stress.

Team / coaching note. You shape your team's primary appraisal. Framing a hard quarter as a threat ("if we miss this we're in trouble") triggers defensive, narrowed, risk-averse behavior; framing it as a challenge ("this is a hard, winnable problem and here's what we'll gain") triggers approach and creativity - provided you also bolster secondary appraisal by visibly supplying resources and support so the challenge is actually copable. Challenge framing without resources is just a threat with a smile.

Core idea - the three dimensions. Burnout is a prolonged response to chronic job stressors, defined by three dimensions (Maslach - Job Burnout, Annual Reviews; Maslach Burnout Inventory - Mind Garden):
Exhaustion - depleted emotional and physical energy (the stress dimension).
Cynicism / depersonalization - negative, detached, callous attitude toward the work and the people in it (the disengagement dimension).
Reduced professional efficacy / inefficacy - a sense of incompetence and unproductiveness; feeling you're no longer making a difference.
Maslach's key insight: burnout is not just exhaustion. Someone tired but still engaged isn't burned out; the cynicism and inefficacy are what make it burnout.

Work engagement - the positive pole. Engagement is the opposite profile: high energy (vs exhaustion), high involvement (vs cynicism), high efficacy (vs inefficacy). "Energy turns into exhaustion, involvement turns into cynicism, efficacy turns into ineffectiveness." So burnout is an erosion of engagement, and the goal isn't merely "less burnout" but building engagement (Burnout and work engagement: the JD-R approach).
The Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model - the causal engine. Every job has two kinds of conditions:
Job demands - workload, time pressure, emotional load, role conflict, etc. Chronic high demands drive the health-impairment path → exhaustion → burnout.

Job resources - autonomy, feedback, social support, growth opportunities, meaningful work, etc. Resources drive the motivational path → engagement, and they also buffer the impact of demands. Burnout, in JD-R terms, is what happens when demands chronically exceed resources. The lever is not just "reduce demands" (often impossible) but increase resources (Schaufeli & Bakker - JD-R, PDF). The six classic areas of work-life mismatch (Maslach & Leiter) name where demands/resources go wrong: workload, control, reward, community, fairness, and values.

Self-management note. Watch for the cynicism signal, not just tiredness - growing detachment and "why bother" is the early-warning light that distinguishes burnout from ordinary fatigue. Audit your own job along the six mismatches (workload, control, reward, community, fairness, values) to locate which resource is depleted, and protect/grow it (claim autonomy, seek feedback and meaning, rebuild support) rather than just trying to rest your way out of a structural deficit.

Team / coaching note. Burnout is primarily an organizational/job-design problem, not an individual resilience failure - Maslach is emphatic that putting the fix entirely on the worker ("be more resilient") is both wrong and unjust. Manage the JD-R balance: where you can't cut demands, deliberately add resources - autonomy, recognition, social support, clear priorities, fairness, and connection to purpose. Diagnose along the six mismatch areas to find the real driver. And treat rising cynicism on the team as a leading indicator of burnout risk, not an attitude problem to discipline.

facets.title: 10. Resilience & recovery — protecting the long game

facts.text: Core idea. Resilience is the capacity to maintain or regain functioning in the face of adversity - to bend without breaking and bounce back. It is not a rare trait; it's an ordinary, trainable set of protective factors: social support, adaptive coping, optimism/realistic self-awareness, and hardiness (Resilience factors - Grand Rising).

Recovery (Sonnentag) - the daily/weekly mechanism. Resilience over time depends on recovery from work stress. Sonnentag & Fritz (2007) identify four recovery experiences that restore the resources work depletes:

Psychological detachment - mentally switching off from work (not just being physically away). The most consistently powerful recovery experience; it's not enough to leave the office if your mind is still in the meeting.
Relaxation - low-activation, low-effort states (a walk, music, rest).
Mastery experiences - off-work challenges that build competence (a hobby, learning something) - restores via accomplishment, not idleness.

Control - deciding how you spend your own off time. Detachment most reliably predicts vitality and well-being; chronic failure to detach (always-on, ruminating) is a direct path toward exhaustion (Sonnentag & Fritz 2007, REQ - PubMed; Stressor-detachment model, Sonnentag 2015).

Post-traumatic growth (Tedeschi & Calhoun) - beyond bouncing back. Some people, after struggling with major adversity, report positive transformation along five domains: personal strength, relating to others, appreciation of life, new possibilities, and spiritual/existential change. Critically, PTG is distinct from resilience: resilience is resistance to / recovery from harm (returning to baseline), whereas PTG is growth beyond the prior baseline - it comes through the struggle and cognitive processing, not from avoiding distress. (Counterintuitively, very high resilience can mean less PTG, because the highly resilient person isn't shaken enough to reconstruct their assumptions) (Tedeschi & Calhoun - PTG overview; Resilience vs PTG, PMC).

Self-management note. Build recovery into the cadence, don't wait for collapse. The most effective move is psychological detachment - a real mental off-switch between work and rest (kill notifications, a shutdown ritual, no email rumination at dinner). Physical time off without mental detachment doesn't recover you. Add relaxation, off-work mastery (a hobby that grows competence), and control over your own time. After a genuinely hard period, leave room for sense-making - growth often comes through the difficulty, not from skipping past it.

Team / coaching note. Recovery is a performance input, not slack to be cut. Protect your team's detachment: model and enforce real off-hours (no "quick" after-hours pings that re-engage the mind), discourage always-on availability, and treat sustainable pace as a productivity strategy. Resilience-building belongs alongside - never instead of - fixing the job demands that cause the strain (see §9). After a crunch or incident, build in genuine recovery and a reflective debrief; that's where both recovery and post-traumatic growth happen.
These ten constructs interlock. A practical sequence for sustaining your own and your team's performance:

Frame ability and goals well (mindset §1, achievement goals §5) - process over person, mastery-approach over performance-avoidance. (But don't expect a "mindset intervention" to do heavy lifting - §1 effect sizes are small.)
Frame the work to fit motivation (regulatory focus §6) - promotion frame for exploration/growth, prevention frame for accuracy-critical work; create regulatory fit.
Build confidence through real wins (self-efficacy §4) - sequence mastery experiences, use peer models, reappraise arousal.
Engineer deep work (flow §3) - challenge-skill match, clear goals, fast feedback, protected focus blocks.

Manage pressure by appraisal, not grit (stress §8, self-regulation §7) - reframe threat as challenge, match coping to controllability, design the environment to reduce the need for willpower (don't budget a mythical fuel tank).
Protect the system from burnout (burnout/JD-R §9) - balance demands with resources; watch cynicism as the early signal; fix job design, don't just tell people to cope.
Recover deliberately (recovery/resilience §10) - psychological detachment first; build recovery and reflection into the cadence as a performance input.

The meta-lesson and the honesty check: the strongest interventions are the structural ones - job design (JD-R), recovery, challenge-skill matching, and engineering genuine mastery experiences. The popular "just be grittier / fix your mindset / use more willpower" advice is exactly where the evidence is weakest (§1, §2, §7). When in doubt, change the system before you exhort the person.

Use this prompt (on yourself, a report, or a team situation) to route a performance, motivation, or burnout problem to the right construct and intervention. It is deliberately structured to force honest, evidence-weighted recommendations.
Treating growth mindset as a high-impact lever. Average intervention effects are tiny (d≈0.08). Useful as a framing default; not a performance program.
"False growth mindset" / blaming. Using "you just need a growth mindset" or "you lack grit" to put structural failures on the individual. Demotivating and unjust.
Screening or labeling people by grit. It mostly re-measures conscientiousness and adds little incremental prediction (Credé 2017).
Budgeting "willpower" as a finite fuel tank. Ego depletion failed to replicate (Hagger 2016). Design the environment to reduce the need for self-control instead.
Threat framing without resources. Telling a team a goal is do-or-die without bolstering their coping resources triggers defensive, narrowed performance.
A purely normative/comparative climate. Stack-ranking and leaderboards push doubters into performance-avoidance (fear, self-handicapping, hidden mistakes).
Treating burnout as an individual resilience deficit. It's primarily a job- design (JD-R) problem; "be more resilient" without fixing demands/resources fails.
Cutting recovery to boost output. Recovery (esp. psychological detachment) is a performance input; always-on availability erodes it and accelerates burnout.
Confusing time-off with recovery. Physical time away without mental detachment doesn't restore you.

facets.title: When to use a different skill (SKIP)

facts.text: Driving a CUSTOMER to adopt a product or build a usage habit - SDT, Fogg B=MAP, stages-of-change, habit loops, adoption goal-setting → behavior-change-psychology. (It touches self-efficacy via decisional balance; this skill owns the self-efficacy construct in depth - §4.)

The LEARNING science of building skill - deliberate practice mechanics, cognitive load, retrieval practice, spacing, interleaving, the illusion of fluency → learning-and-expertise-psychology. (This skill owns the motivational and performance drivers; that one owns how skill is acquired.)

Emotion-regulation MECHANICS & emotional intelligence - Gross's process model, reappraisal vs suppression, EI, affect → emotion-and-affect-psychology. (This skill owns stress/coping/burnout/resilience; that one owns the regulation toolkit - see §8 cross-reference.)

Team trust, rapport & psychological SAFETY between people - Edmondson, the Trust Equation, repairing trust after a breach → trust-and-psychological-safety. (This skill owns individual resilience/burnout; that one owns team safety.)
Cognitive biases, prospect theory, replication-crisis methodology, and ego depletion as a DECISION-effect → behavioral-decision-making (see §7 cross-reference).
Attitude-change theory - ELM, cognitive dissonance, reactance → persuasion-and-influence-psychology.
Trust in / appropriate reliance on AI tools → human-ai-interaction-psychology.
